title: Deflated-RankICIR: Multiple-Testing-Aware Factor Selection for LLM-Driven Alpha Mining

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to correct multiple testing bias (winner's curse) when selecting factors from large LLM-mined candidate pools ranked by uncorrected validation metrics. Papers [1], [2], [3], [5], and [19] all address correcting selection bias and backtest overfitting in financial contexts, specifically using the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) framework. While these papers focus on strategy selection rather than factor selection, the underlying objective — mitigating performance inflation due to selection bias — is substantively equivalent. Paper [6] also addresses selection bias under multiple testing but uses an unsupervised learning method rather than DSR. Paper [9] introduces a factor-adjusted multiple testing procedure for mutual fund selection, which is conceptually similar but operates in a different statistical framework. Overall, the purpose is covered by prior work.

### Mechanism
The contribution adapts the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) framework to factor-level RankIC time series, creating Deflated-RankICIR. Papers [1], [2], [3], [5], and [19] introduce and apply the DSR framework to correct for selection bias and backtest overfitting in financial strategy selection. The mechanism of DSR — computing the probability that observed performance metrics reflect genuine predictive power rather than selection bias — is directly equivalent to the mechanism of Deflated-RankICIR, as both rely on the same statistical primitive. The adaptation to RankIC time series does not constitute a new mechanism, as it is merely a domain-specific application of the same statistical tool.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves comparing the Deflated-RankICIR method against a RankICIR baseline and other selection methods using metrics like Information Ratio and Calmar Ratio on CSI300 with 70 LLM-mined factors. Papers [1], [2], [3], [5], and [19] use similar evaluation designs to validate DSR, including comparisons against baselines and performance metrics like Sharpe Ratio. Paper [10] evaluates multiple testing methods in finance using similar statistical comparisons. While the specific dataset (CSI300) and factors are new, the evaluation design — comparing methods using standard financial performance metrics — is covered by prior work.

### Domain
The domain is quantitative finance, specifically LLM-driven alpha mining. Papers [1], [2], [3], [5], [6], [9], [10], [15], and [17] all operate within the general domain of quantitative finance and factor selection for asset pricing or investment strategies. While the specific focus on LLM-mined factors is new, this is a narrower instance within the established domain of quantitative finance. Therefore, the domain is covered.

### Per-Facet Reasoning:

#### Purpose:
The contribution identifies why analytical standard error formulas are inadequate for ranking factors under estimation uncertainty. This specific empirical relationship — the inadequacy of analytical formulas for ranking factors — does not appear in any prior paper. While papers like [6] and [8] discuss uncertainty in ranking, they do not address the inadequacy of analytical standard error formulas for ranking factors under estimation uncertainty. Similarly, papers like [15] and [23] discuss bootstrap standard error estimation but do not establish the same relationship between analytical formulas and ranking inadequacy.

#### Mechanism:
The contribution uses the stationary bootstrap to estimate per-factor standard errors instead of analytical formulas that produce near-constant estimates. Papers [3], [4], [5], [7], [18], and [28] all discuss the stationary bootstrap as a resampling method for estimating standard errors in various contexts, including weakly dependent stationary observations and time series models. The mechanism of using the stationary bootstrap for standard error estimation is therefore covered.

#### Evaluation:
The evaluation demonstrates that bootstrap-based estimation creates meaningful rank differentiation (Spearman correlation 0.83 between DSR and RankICIR), whereas analytical formulas fail to distinguish factors. Papers [6], [8], and [10] discuss rank uncertainty and differentiation under various conditions, but none use the same evaluation design (Spearman correlation between DSR and RankICIR). Additionally, no prior paper evaluates the differentiation of ranks specifically in the context of bootstrap-based versus analytical standard error estimation. The evaluation design appears novel.

#### Domain:
The contribution operates in the domain of quantitative finance, specifically LLM-driven alpha mining. Papers [24], [25], [26], and [31] all address quantitative finance and related applications, including portfolio optimization, Sharpe ratio analysis, and trading strategies. The domain is therefore covered.
